body.heading: What an ice age is
paragraphs: Strictly, an ice age is any long period when Earth carries permanent ice sheets — which means, by that definition, we are in one now, since Greenland and Antarctica remain ice-covered. The famous 'ice ages' of popular imagination are the glacial periods within it, when the ice advanced far across the continents, most recently peaking about 20,000 years ago.

During that peak, global sea level sat roughly 120 metres lower than today, because so much water was locked up as land ice. Britain was joined to Europe by dry land, and Siberia to Alaska, along routes early humans and animals used.

body.heading: The slow metronome
paragraphs: Glacial periods come and go on rhythms of tens of thousands of years, paced by slow wobbles in Earth's orbit and tilt that change how sunlight is distributed — the Milankovitch cycles. Small cooling at key latitudes lets snow survive the summer; bright ice reflects more sunlight, cooling things further, and the feedback builds an ice sheet.

The warm intervals between glacial periods, like the one we live in, typically last about ten to fifteen thousand years. Ice ages are not ancient exceptions in Earth's story. For much of the planet's recent history, ice has been a regular, returning character.

takeaway: Ice ages are long cold eras paced by Earth's orbital wobbles, when ice sheets advanced and seas fell dramatically.
